contributions: Proves the theorem that any GNN with the standard message-passing update rule cannot distinguish graphs that the 1-WL test cannot distinguish (Xu et al., 2019)
Derives GIN as the unique 1-WL-equivalent GNN, establishing sum aggregation with a (1+ε) self-loop term and an expressive MLP as necessary and sufficient conditions
Characterizes over-squashing through the Cheeger constant and provides a formal Jacobian bound showing exponential decay of long-range influence
Establishes permutation equivariance and over-squashing as the two fundamental theoretical constraints on message-passing networks
limitations: 1-WL cannot count cycles, triangles, or detect general subgraph patterns—fundamental limits not fixable by training
Regular graphs are indistinguishable by any standard MPNN regardless of depth or parameters
The k-WL hierarchy is computationally intractable for k≥3 on large graphs
Over-squashing is inherent to dense-graph message passing; remedies like graph rewiring or transformers introduce additional complexity or cost
Sum aggregation's theoretical injectivity assumes a countable domain; practical MLP approximation may not achieve full expressiveness
methods: The chapter presents rigorous proofs using induction on GNN layer depth to show the equivalence between 1-WL color refinement and MPNN updates. It analyzes aggregation function properties (injectivity on multisets) to derive why sum works while mean and max fail. Over-squashing is characterized formally using the Jacobian of the K-layer GNN output with respect to distant inputs, bounded by Lipschitz constants and degree products along paths. The Cheeger constant is used to quantify graph bottlenecks causing over-squashing.
results: 1-WL always terminates in at most |V| iterations since distinct colors are bounded by |V|
GCN mean aggregation collapses distinct multisets (e.g., {1,0},{1,0} and {2,0} both yield [1,0]); max aggregation also loses multiplicity information

GIN with sum aggregation and an MLP of at least two layers achieves full 1-WL expressiveness; the (1+ε) self-loop term is necessary to prevent different neighborhood sizes from producing identical sums
1-WL fails on d-regular graphs with the same number of nodes, including the canonical pair K_{3,3} and the triangular prism (both 3-regular on 6 nodes)
Over-squashing Jacobian bound: ||∂h_v^(K)/∂x_u|| ≤ C^K · ∏(1/deg(v_k)), showing exponential decay along paths through high-degree nodes
k-WL computational cost grows as O(n^k · d^k), making k=3 impractical even for moderate graphs (e.g., ~4.8×10^15 triples for ogbn-arxiv)
tldr: Message-passing GNNs are provably bounded by the 1-WL color refinement test in expressiveness, with GIN being the unique architecture achieving this upper bound via injective sum aggregation. Two fundamental failure modes—over-squashing and over-smoothing—constrain practical performance beyond this theoretical ceiling.
